title: Cryptography Fundamentals
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 3: Security Architecture and Engineering: Cryptography Fundamentals.

items: Uses one shared key for both encryption and decryption
Fast and efficient for bulk data encryption
Key distribution is the biggest challenge
Number of keys needed = n(n-1)/2 where n = number of users
Provides confidentiality but NOT authentication or non-repudiation

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: "Symmetric key algorithms can provide confidentiality, but not authentication or nonrepudiation." From Chapple: "Symmetric key cryptography has several weaknesses: Key distribution is a major problem. Parties must have a secure method of exchanging the secret key before establishing communications." Block vs. Stream Ciphers:

items: Block cipher — Encrypts fixed-size blocks of data (AES, DES)
Stream cipher — Encrypts data bit by bit or byte by byte (RC4)

blocks.text: Confusion and Diffusion: From Chapple: "Cryptographic algorithms rely on two basic operations: confusion (making the relationship between key and ciphertext complex) and diffusion (spreading plaintext influence across the ciphertext)." ⚠️ Exam Trap: AES is the current standard. Know that AES uses 128-bit blocks (not 64-bit like DES). AES key sizes are 128, 192, or 256 bits.

items: Uses key pair — public key (shared) and private key (secret)
Slower than symmetric but solves key distribution problem
Provides confidentiality, authentication, and non-repudiation
Number of keys needed = 2n where n = number of users
Foundation for digital signatures and PKI

blocks.text: From Chapple: "RSA is the most commonly used asymmetric algorithm, and its strength has had to continue to increase to mitigate advancements in processing technology." Comparison:
Hybrid cryptosystems combine both: asymmetric encryption exchanges a symmetric session key, which is then used for bulk data encryption. This is how TLS/HTTPS works.

items: Produces fixed-length output (digest/hash) from any input
One-way function — cannot reverse the hash to get the original data
Used for integrity verification, password storage, digital signatures
Must be collision-resistant (hard to find two inputs with same hash)
Hashing does NOT provide confidentiality (no key involved)

blocks.text: From Chapple: "The Secure Hash Algorithm SHA-3 is the government standard. They must allow input of any length, provide fixed-length output, make it relatively easy to compute the hash function for any input, provide one-way functionality, and be collision-resistant." HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code): Combines a hash with a secret key to provide both integrity AND authentication. HMAC-SHA256 is commonly used. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Hashing provides INTEGRITY, not confidentiality. If a hash value changes, the data has been modified. But hashing alone doesn't tell you WHO modified it (HMAC adds that).

items: Created by encrypting hash with sender's private key
Provides integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation
Verified using sender's public key
Does NOT provide confidentiality (the message itself is not encrypted)
Combined with encryption for full CIA protection
Sender creates hash of the message
Sender encrypts hash with their private key → digital signature
Sender sends message + signature
Recipient decrypts signature with sender's public key → reveals hash
Recipient hashes the received message independently
If hashes match → integrity confirmed, authentication confirmed
Integrity — Hash verifies data hasn't been modified
Authentication — Only the private key holder could create the signature
Non-repudiation — Sender cannot deny sending (their private key was used)

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Digital signatures are created with the PRIVATE key and verified with the PUBLIC key. This is the opposite of encryption (encrypt with public, decrypt with private).

items: PKI — Framework for managing digital certificates and public keys
Certificate Authority (CA) — Issues and manages certificates
Registration Authority (RA) — Verifies identity before CA issues certificate
Certificate Revocation List (CRL) — List of revoked certificates
OCSP — Online Certificate Status Protocol (real-time revocation checking)

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP (Figure 3-60): PKI components include CA, RA, digital certificates, CRL, and key management systems. X.509 Certificate Contents:

items: Version, Serial number
Signature algorithm
Issuer (CA)
Validity period (not before, not after)
Subject (certificate holder)
Public key
Extensions
Digital signature of the CA

blocks.text: Certificate Pinning: From Chapple: "If a malicious actor is sitting between the web server and the user, the malicious actor might send a spoofed certificate. Certificate pinning offers a means by which this possibility can be avoided." ⚠️ Exam Trap: A certificate does NOT contain the private key. It contains the public key and is signed by the CA's private key.

items: Brute Force — Try every possible key (countered by longer keys)
Birthday Attack — Exploits hash collisions (probability math)
Man-in-the-Middle — Intercept and alter communications
Known Plaintext — Attacker has both plaintext and ciphertext
Chosen Plaintext/Ciphertext — Attacker can choose inputs for analysis

rows: Attack double encryption from both ends

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Birthday attacks exploit the mathematics behind the birthday problem (probability of two people sharing a birthday in a group)." From Shon Harris: "Social engineering techniques can also be used in cryptanalysis." ⚠️ Exam Trap: The birthday attack works against HASHING, not encryption. It exploits the probability of finding collisions. A hash function with n-bit output can be birthday-attacked with approximately 2^(n/2) attempts.
